mainTopic: Praying while needing to relieve oneself, and handling תפילין near a בית הכסא (ברכות כג.)
overview: The גמרא finishes explaining the dispute between רב חסדא and רב המנונא about someone who stopped his תפילה to urinate. רב אשי shows that everyone agrees a long pause means starting over. The real question is whether the person was fit to pray at all (גברא חזיא or גברא דחויא). A ברייתא teaches that one who needs to relieve himself may not pray, but only if he cannot wait as long as it takes to walk a פרסה. רבי יונתן finds a source in "הכון לקראת אלהיך", and the גמרא explains "שמור רגלך" in two ways: about sin, קרבנות and תשובה, and about guarding one's body during תפילה. The גמרא then turns to תפילין and the בית הכסא: removing them four אמות away, not entering with them even to urinate, and where to keep them. After a tragic story and a history of failed resting spots, the חכמים enacted that one holds them, rolled up in the hand and covered by the garment. Further rules cover using a pouch at night, the size of that pouch, and רבי יוחנן's practice of keeping his תפילין with him; his reason continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A first suggestion: they argue about how long a delay requires starting over
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that רב חסדא and רב המנונא argue about someone who paused long enough to finish the whole תפילה. One says he goes back to the beginning, the other says he goes back to where he stopped.
steps.simpleTranslation: One master holds: if he paused long enough to finish the whole prayer, he goes back to the beginning. The other master holds: he goes back to where he stopped.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a proposed explanation of what רב חסדא and רב המנונא argue about. The suggestion is that they disagree about a general rule for long pauses in תפילה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, these two אמוראים argued about someone who stopped his תפילה to urinate. One said he starts over, the other said he continues from where he stopped. The suggestion here is that their argument is really a general one about long pauses, and does not depend on the bathroom issue.

keyTerms.meaning: Long enough to finish the whole prayer
To the place where he stopped

phrases.english: One master holds: if he paused

phrases.aramaic: כְּדֵי לִגְמוֹר אֶת כּוּלָּהּ — חוֹזֵר לָרֹאשׁ.
phrases.english: long enough to finish all of it, he returns to the beginning.
phrases.notes: "All of it" means the whole תפילה (שמונה עשרה).

phrases.english: And the other master holds: he returns to the place where he stopped.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר סָבַר: אִם שָׁהָה כְּדֵי לִגְמוֹר אֶת כּוּלָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the proposed explanation (לימא בהא קמיפלגי) that began on the previous amud.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The dispute is about whether a pause long enough to finish the whole תפילה requires starting over.

steps.title: רב אשי rejects the suggestion: the case never mentions the length of the pause
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי argues that if the dispute were about long pauses, the case would have mentioned pausing versus not pausing. Since it does not, that cannot be the real issue.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: about this 'if he paused', they should have needed to discuss 'if he did not pause'!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי pushes back on the suggestion from step 1. He says it does not match how the original dispute was worded.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the argument were really about long pauses, we would expect the case to separate 'paused long' from 'did not pause long'. The original dispute says nothing about the length of the pause. So the suggested explanation does not fit the case.

keyTerms.meaning: A late Babylonian אמורא, often a key editor of the Talmud
He should have needed to say this

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
This matter of 'if he paused',
then 'if he did not pause' should also have been needed!
phrases.notes: In other words, the dispute should have been worded around the length of the pause, and it was not.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: הַאי ״אִם שָׁהָה״, אִם לֹא שָׁהָה מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the explanation offered in step 1.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole suggestion that the dispute is about long pauses.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The original case does not separate long and short pauses, so the dispute cannot be about pause length.

steps.title: רב אשי's explanation: everyone agrees about long pauses; the dispute is about a short one
steps.stepSummary: Everyone agrees that a pause long enough to finish the whole תפילה means starting over. The dispute is about a shorter pause. One view holds that the person was unfit to pray from the start (גברא דחויא), so his תפילה does not count. The other holds that he was fit (גברא חזיא), so it counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, everyone agrees that if he paused long enough to finish the whole prayer, he goes back to the beginning. Their dispute is about where he did not pause that long. One master holds he is a disqualified man, not fit, and his prayer is not a prayer. The other master holds he is a fit man, and his prayer is a prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a new explanation of the dispute between רב חסדא and רב המנונא. It is about the status of the person who prayed, not about pause length.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The long-pause rule is now agreed by everyone. For a short pause, the question is whether needing to urinate made the person unfit to pray from the start. If he was unfit, what he already said is worthless and he must start over. If he was fit, his words count and he continues from where he stopped.
steps.whatToRemember: A long pause (long enough to finish the whole תפילה) means starting over, according to everyone. After a short pause, the question is whether the person who needed to relieve himself was fit to pray at all (גברא חזיא or גברא דחויא).
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two issues. The length of the pause is not disputed at all. The dispute is only about the person's fitness during a short pause.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the idea, developed in the ברייתא that follows, that a bodily need can make a person unfit for תפילה.

phrases.english: Rather, according to everyone,

phrases.aramaic: אִם שָׁהָה כְּדֵי לִגְמוֹר אֶת כּוּלָּהּ — חוֹזֵר לָרֹאשׁ,
phrases.english: if he paused long enough to finish all of it, he returns to the beginning,
and there, they disagree about where he did not pause that long,
for one master holds he is a disqualified man,
and not fit, and his prayer is not a prayer.
phrases.notes: So he must start the תפילה over from the beginning.

phrases.english: And the other master holds he is a fit man,
and his prayer is a prayer.
phrases.notes: So he continues from where he stopped.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected explanation from step 1 with a new one.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframing the dispute (shifting the point of disagreement)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The dispute is about how a long pause affects תפילה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Everyone agrees about long pauses. After a short pause, they argue whether the person was fit (גברא חזיא) or unfit (גברא דחויא) to pray.

steps.title: ברייתא: one who needs to relieve himself may not pray
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a person who needs to relieve himself may not pray. If he did pray, his תפילה is a תועבה (abomination).
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: one who needs to relieve himself should not pray, and if he prayed, his prayer is an abomination.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source, a ברייתא, about praying while needing to relieve oneself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This goes further than the case of stopping in the middle. Here the person began praying while already needing the bathroom. The language is very strong: his תפילה is called a תועבה.

keyTerms.meaning: One who needs to relieve himself

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who needs to relieve himself should not pray,
and if he prayed, his prayer is an abomination.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a related ברייתא about praying while needing to relieve oneself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who needs to relieve himself may not pray, and if he did, his תפילה is a תועבה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basic source for the halacha that one should not pray while needing the bathroom.

steps.title: Limitation: this applies only if he cannot hold himself in
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד (some say רב יהודה) limits the ברייתא. It applies only to someone who cannot hold himself in. If he can hold himself in, his תפילה is valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד, and some say רב יהודה, said: they only taught this when he cannot hold himself in. But if he can hold himself in, his prayer is a valid prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא narrows the harsh rule of the ברייתא to one specific situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The label תועבה is limited to someone whose need is urgent. A person who feels a mild need but can wait comfortably is not disqualified. His תפילה counts.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this in the case of

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב זְבִיד וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב יְהוּדָה:
phrases.english: Rav Zevid, and some say Rav Yehuda, said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לִשְׁהוֹת בְּעַצְמוֹ,
phrases.english: They only taught this when he cannot hold himself in,
but if he can hold himself in,
his prayer is a valid prayer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the ברייתא from step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ברייתא applies only to someone who cannot hold himself in. Someone who can hold himself in may pray, and his תפילה is valid.

steps.title: How long must he be able to hold himself in?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how long a person must be able to wait to count as 'able to hold himself in'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And for how long?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a measurement. It is setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Able to hold himself in' is vague. The גמרא wants a clear standard so a person knows whether he may pray.

keyTerms.meaning: And up to how much (how long)?

phrases.english: And for how long?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the measurement behind the limitation in step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How long a person must be able to wait for his תפילה to be valid.

steps.title: רב ששת: up to a פרסה
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת answers that the measure is a פרסה, meaning the time it takes to walk one parasang.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: up to a פרסה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers the question from step 6 with a set measurement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the person could wait as long as it takes to walk a פרסה, he counts as able to hold himself in, and his תפילה is valid. If he could not wait that long, the ברייתא's rule applies.

keyTerms.meaning: Parasang, a distance of about 4 מיל; here it measures the time needed to walk it

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said: up to a parasang.
phrases.notes: This is the time it takes to walk one parasang.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He must be able to wait as long as it takes to walk a פרסה.

steps.title: Another version: the limitation is part of the ברייתא itself
steps.stepSummary: Some teach the limitation as part of the ברייתא itself, not as a statement by an אמורא. The rule applies only when he cannot hold himself in. If he can, his תפילה is valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some teach it on the ברייתא itself: when is this said? When he cannot hold himself in. But if he can hold himself in, his prayer is a valid prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא records a second version of the same teaching. In this version, the limitation comes from the ברייתא itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The halacha is the same in both versions. What changes is who said it. In this version the limitation is a ברייתא, a source from the תנאים, which gives it more authority than an אמורא's comment.

keyTerms.meaning: On the ברייתא (the teaching of the תנאים)
In what case are these words said?
To control himself, hold himself in

phrases.english: Some teach this directly on the baraita:
In what case is this said?
When he cannot hold himself in.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אִם יָכוֹל לַעֲמוֹד עַל עַצְמוֹ —
phrases.english: But if he can hold himself in,
his prayer is a valid prayer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of step 5, placing the limitation inside the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the ברייתא itself, the rule applies only to someone who cannot hold himself in.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new disagreement about the halacha. It is the same rule, recorded with a different source.

steps.title: In this version, רב זביד sets the measure at a פרסה
steps.stepSummary: In the second version, the same question is asked, and רב זביד answers: up to a פרסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And for how long? רב זביד said: up to a פרסה.
steps.whatsHappening: The second version ends with the same question and the same measurement. Here the answer is credited to רב זביד instead of רב ששת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both versions agree that the measure is a פרסה. What differs is who said what. In the first version, רב זביד (or רב יהודה) stated the limitation and רב ששת gave the measure. In this version, the limitation is part of the ברייתא itself, and רב זביד is the one who gives the measure.
steps.whatToRemember: A person who needs to relieve himself may not pray. If he cannot hold himself in, his תפילה is a תועבה. If he can wait as long as it takes to walk a פרסה, his תפילה is valid.

phrases.english: And for how long?
Rav Zevid said: up to a parasang.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעַד כַּמָּה? אָמַר רַב זְבִיד: עַד פַּרְסָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the second version by giving its measurement.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Up to a פרסה, according to רב זביד.

steps.title: Do not pray when you need to relieve yourself
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני, quoting רבי יונתן, rules that someone who needs to relieve himself should not pray. The source is the פסוק "הכון לקראת אלהיך ישראל".
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: A person who needs to relieve himself should not pray, because the פסוק says, "Prepare to meet your God, O Israel."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new אמורא's ruling that a person who needs to go to the bathroom should not pray. It gives a פסוק as the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now, the סוגיא worked from a ברייתא and asked how long a person must be able to hold himself in. Here the rule gets a source in the פסוק: "הכון" means you must be properly prepared to stand before ה׳. Someone who is uncomfortable and distracted by his body is not prepared.

keyTerms.meaning: One who needs to relieve himself (literally, "needs his openings")

steps.whyThisMatters: This step gives the source for the הלכה that a person must not pray while he urgently needs the bathroom. תפילה requires being ready, in body and mind, to stand before ה׳.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said
Rabbi Yonatan said:
One who needs to relieve himself —
should not pray,
because it says:
"Prepare to meet your God, O Israel."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the topic of praying while needing to relieve oneself and gives it a source in the פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who needs to relieve himself may not pray, because of "הכון לקראת אלהיך".

steps.title: Guard yourself from sin, and if you sin, bring an offering
steps.stepSummary: In a second statement from the same chain, רבי יונתן explains "שמור רגלך כאשר תלך אל בית האלהים". It means: guard yourself from sin, and if you do sin, bring a קרבן before ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני also said in the name of רבי יונתן: What does the פסוק mean, "Guard your foot when you go to the house of God"? It means: guard yourself so you do not sin. If you do sin, bring a קרבן before Me.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching from the same chain of rabbis. This one explains a פסוק about coming to the house of God.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words "מאי דכתיב" open an explanation of a פסוק. They are not a challenge. "Guard your foot" is read as "guard yourself" from sin. When a person goes to the בית המקדש after a sin, he should come with a קרבן.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the meaning of what is written? (opens an explanation of a פסוק)
The house of God (the בית המקדש)
An offering brought in the בית המקדש

steps.confusionAlert: "מאי דכתיב" looks like a question, but it is not a קשיא. It is a standard way to begin explaining a פסוק.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said
that Rabbi Yonatan said:
What is the meaning of what is written:
"Guard your foot when you go
to the house of God"?
Guard yourself so that you do not sin,
and if you do sin —
bring an offering before Me.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן: מַאי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brought here because it comes from the same chain of rabbis and also deals with coming before ה׳.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: "שמור רגלך" means guard yourself from sin, and if you sin, bring a קרבן.

steps.title: Be like the wise who repent, not like fools who only bring offerings
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains the next words of the פסוק. Listen to the חכמים, who bring a קרבן and also do תשובה. Do not be like the fools, who bring a קרבן without doing תשובה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק continues: "And come close to listen to the words of the wise." רבא said: Be close to hearing the words of the wise, who, when they sin, bring a קרבן and also do תשובה. Then the פסוק says: "It is better than when fools give sacrifices." This means: do not be like the fools, who sin and bring a קרבן but do not do תשובה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא continues explaining the same פסוק, piece by piece. He contrasts wise people with fools.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new point is that a קרבן alone is not enough. The wise person brings a קרבן and also does תשובה. The fool only brings the animal and does not change.
steps.whyThisMatters: This teaches a basic idea: a קרבן does not work automatically. It has to come together with real תשובה.

phrases.english: "And come close to listen to the words of the wise,"
phrases.notes: The פסוק itself says only "to listen"; "words of the wise" is the גמרא's explanation.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Be close to hearing the words of the wise,
who, if they sin,
bring an offering and repent.
"It is better than when fools give sacrifices" —
do not be like the fools
who sin and bring an offering,
but do not repent.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: הֱוֵי קָרוֹב לִשְׁמוֹעַ דִּבְרֵי חֲכָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues explaining the same פסוק from קהלת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wise people bring a קרבן and do תשובה; fools bring a קרבן without תשובה.

steps.title: If they don't know how to do evil, they would be righteous
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the end of the פסוק, "כי אינם יודעים לעשות רע". If the fools do not know how to do evil, that would make them צדיקים, not fools.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק ends: "For they do not know how to do evil." If so, they are righteous!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reaches the last words of the פסוק and points out a problem. Read simply, these words seem to praise the fools.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "They do not know how to do evil" sounds like a description of good people. That cannot fit people the פסוק has just called fools. So the simple reading must be wrong.

phrases.english: "For they do not know how to do evil"
If so, they are righteous!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the meaning of the final words of the פסוק being explained.
steps.kashyaTarget: The simple reading of "כי אינם יודעים לעשות רע"
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Not knowing how to do evil describes צדיקים, so it cannot describe fools.

steps.title: Fools who cannot tell whether their offering is for good or bad
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the fools do not know whether they are bringing their קרבן for something good, as a thanks offering, or for something bad, as atonement. הקדוש ברוך הוא complains: they cannot tell good from bad, yet they bring Me offerings?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means: do not be like the fools who sin and bring a קרבן, but do not know whether they are bringing it for the good or for the bad. הקדוש ברוך הוא said: They cannot tell good from bad, and they bring a קרבן before Me?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by reading the words differently. "They do not know evil" means they cannot recognize what is evil.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At first the words seemed to mean the fools are innocent of evil. Now they mean the fools are clueless about evil. They do not even know whether their own actions were good or bad, so their קרבן has no real meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: The Holy One, Blessed be He

steps.whatToRemember: The פסוק in קהלת teaches that a קרבן is meaningful only when it comes with תשובה and with understanding of what one did wrong. A fool who cannot tell good from bad gains nothing from bringing it.

phrases.english: Rather: do not be like the fools
who sin and bring an offering,
but do not know
whether they are bringing it for the good,
or whether they are bringing it for the bad.
The Holy One, Blessed be He, said:
They cannot tell between good and bad,
and they bring an offering before Me?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by reinterpreting the final words of the פסוק.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: "They do not know how to do evil" means they are innocent of evil.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means they cannot recognize evil, so they do not know whether their קרבן is for good or for bad.

steps.title: Guard your body's openings when you pray
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי (or רבי חנינא בר פפא) reads "שמור רגלך" differently: guard your body's openings when you stand in תפילה before ה׳. This connects the פסוק back to the סוגיא's main topic.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי, and some say רבי חנינא בר פפא, said: Guard your body's openings when you stand in תפילה before Me.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא gives a different explanation of "שמור רגלך". It brings the discussion back to needing the bathroom during תפילה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יונתן read "guard your foot" as "guard yourself from sin". Here "foot" is understood as a polite way of referring to the body's openings. The פסוק becomes an instruction to keep the body clean and controlled during תפילה.

keyTerms.meaning: And some say (the statement is attributed to another rabbi)

steps.whatToRemember: There are two readings of "שמור רגלך". One is about guarding yourself from sin and bringing a קרבן with תשובה. The other is about guarding your body during תפילה, which fits the סוגיא's topic of not praying when one needs to relieve himself.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi, and some say
Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa, said:
Guard your openings
when you stand
in prayer before Me.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בַּר פָּפָּא אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different reading of the same פסוק ("שמור רגלך") explained in step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: "שמור רגלך" means guard your body's openings while standing in תפילה.

steps.title: Remove תפילין four אמות before the בית הכסא
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that one who enters a בית הכסא removes his תפילין at a distance of four אמות and then goes in.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: Someone going into a bathroom takes off his תפילין four אמות away, and then goes in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא with a basic rule: take off your תפילין four אמות before you reach the bathroom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סוגיא moves from the earlier topic of תפילה back to practical laws of תפילין and a dirty place. The rule sets a buffer zone of four אמות. The bathroom is not just a place where תפילין may not be worn. Even the area right next to it calls for taking them off.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who enters a bathroom,
removes his tefillin at a distance of four cubits,
and then enters.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic, practical laws of תפילין near a bathroom, after the aggadic discussion of קרבנות and תפילה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One removes תפילין four אמות before entering a בית הכסא.

steps.title: The rule applies only to a permanent bathroom
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת limits the ברייתא to a permanent bathroom. In a makeshift spot, one removes the תפילין and relieves himself right away. On leaving, though, he must go four אמות before putting them back on, because the spot has now become a permanent bathroom.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר רב הונא said in the name of רב ששת: This was taught only about a permanent bathroom. In a makeshift bathroom, one takes off his תפילין and relieves himself right away. When he leaves, he goes four אמות away and puts them back on, because he has now made that spot a permanent bathroom.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא narrows the ברייתא. The four-אמות rule on the way in applies only to a regular, permanent bathroom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A makeshift spot, such as an open field, is not yet a bathroom before it is used, so there is no buffer zone going in. Once he has relieved himself there, the spot counts as a permanent bathroom. So the four-אמות distance applies when he leaves.

keyTerms.meaning: This was only taught regarding (a limiting formula)
And puts them on (here: puts the תפילין back on)

steps.confusionAlert: Here וּמַנִּיחָן means putting the תפילין back ON, not putting them down. He walks four אמות away and only then puts them back on.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת:
phrases.english: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna said in the name of Rav Sheshet:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בֵּית הַכִּסֵּא קָבוּעַ,
phrases.english: They only taught this about a permanent bathroom,
but in a makeshift bathroom,
he removes them and relieves himself immediately.
And when he leaves,
he distances himself four cubits and puts them on,
because he has made it a permanent bathroom.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בֵּית הַכִּסֵּא קָבוּעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the scope of the ברייתא in step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The four-אמות distance on entering applies only to a permanent bathroom. In a makeshift one, it applies only when leaving, once the spot has become permanent.

steps.title: May one enter wearing תפילין just to urinate?
steps.stepSummary: The yeshiva asks whether one may enter a permanent bathroom wearing תפילין if he only needs to urinate.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: May a person go into a permanent bathroom wearing תפילין in order to urinate?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new question that the ברייתא did not address: what is the rule if he only needs to urinate?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Urinating is quicker and less degrading than relieving oneself fully. So perhaps removing the תפילין is not needed. This step sets up the dispute and ruling that follow.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was raised before them

phrases.english: A question was raised before them:
May a person enter wearing tefillin
into a permanent bathroom in order to urinate?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the rule for a permanent bathroom and asks about a lighter case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether one must remove תפילין before entering a permanent bathroom only to urinate.

steps.title: רבינא permits, רב אדא בר מתנא forbids
steps.stepSummary: Two אמוראים disagree. רבינא permits entering with תפילין to urinate, and רב אדא בר מתנא forbids it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא permitted it, and רב אדא בר מתנא forbade it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports that two אמוראים disagreed about the question. This sets up the next step, where they ask רבא to decide.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא holds that urinating is minor, so the תפילין may stay on. רב אדא בר מתנא forbids it, and his reason is spelled out in רבא's ruling.

phrases.english: Ravina permitted,
Rav Adda bar Masna forbade.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבִינָא שָׁרֵי, רַב אַדָּא בַּר מַתְנָא אָסַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Presents the two opinions on the question from step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a dispute: רבינא permits and רב אדא בר מתנא forbids.

steps.title: רבא forbids it out of concern
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that it is forbidden. The worry is that he may end up relieving himself fully with the תפילין on. A second version says the worry is that he may pass wind with them on.
steps.simpleTranslation: They came and asked רבא. He told them: It is forbidden. We are worried he may end up relieving himself fully while wearing them. Some say the worry is that he may pass wind while wearing them.
steps.whatsHappening: The question goes to רבא, who decides like the strict view, and the גמרא gives two versions of his reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a protective rule. Urinating alone might be fine, but once he is in the bathroom he may go further. Both versions share the same idea: the setting makes a real violation likely.
steps.whatToRemember: The final ruling follows רבא: do not enter a permanent bathroom wearing תפילין, even only to urinate.

phrases.english: They came and asked Rava,
he said to them: It is forbidden,
we are concerned lest he relieve himself fully with them on.
And some say: lest he pass wind with them on.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the dispute from step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It is forbidden, out of concern that he will relieve himself fully, or pass wind, while wearing the תפילין.

steps.title: בית שמאי: leave the תפילין in a window
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא gives בית שמאי's view. Remove the תפילין four אמות away, place them in a window facing the public area, and enter. On leaving, go four אמות away and put them back on.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא taught: Someone entering a permanent bathroom takes off his תפילין four אמות away, puts them in the window next to the public area, and goes in. When he comes out, he goes four אמות away and puts them back on. This is the view of בית שמאי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a second ברייתא about what to do with the תפילין while inside, starting with בית שמאי's opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא only said to remove them. This one adds where to keep them. בית שמאי says to leave them outside in a window, so they never enter the bathroom at all.

phrases.english: It was taught in another baraita:
One who enters a permanent bathroom
removes his tefillin at a distance of four cubits,
places them in the window adjacent to the public domain,
and enters.

phrases.aramaic: וּכְשֶׁהוּא יוֹצֵא — מַרְחִיק אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת, וּמַנִּיחָן,
phrases.english: And when he leaves, he distances four cubits and puts them on,
These are the words of Beit Shammai.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a parallel ברייתא that adds where to keep the תפילין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בית שמאי: leave the תפילין in a window facing the public area, then enter.

steps.title: בית הלל: in his hand; רבי עקיבא: in his garment
steps.stepSummary: בית הלל say he holds the תפילין in his hand and enters. רבי עקיבא says he holds them in his garment and enters.
steps.simpleTranslation: בית הלל say: He holds them in his hand and goes in. רבי עקיבא says: He holds them in his garment and goes in.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with two other views. Both allow taking the תפילין inside, as long as they are held.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike בית שמאי, who leave the תפילין outside, בית הלל have him keep them with him, held in his hand. רבי עקיבא says to hold them in his garment, and the גמרא is about to question that wording.

phrases.english: And Beit Hillel say:
He holds them in his hand and enters.
Rabbi Akiva says:
He holds them in his garment and enters.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים: אוֹחֲזָן בְּיָדוֹ, וְנִכְנָס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the other opinions in the same ברייתא, disagreeing with בית שמאי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בית הלל: hold them in the hand. רבי עקיבא: hold them in the garment.

steps.title: Holding תפילין in a garment risks them falling
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי עקיבא's wording. Holding them only in the garment is risky, since he may forget them and they will fall.
steps.simpleTranslation: In his garment, can you really think so? Sometimes he will forget about them and they will fall!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the wording of רבי עקיבא's view as impractical.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the תפילין are just tucked into his clothing, he might forget they are there, and they could fall to the floor of the bathroom. That would be a serious disgrace to the תפילין.

keyTerms.meaning: Could it enter your mind? (a challenge formula)

phrases.english: In his garment, does it enter your mind?!
Sometimes he forgets them and they fall!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי עקיבא's opinion in step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי עקיבא's ruling that one holds the תפילין in his garment.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Tefillin held only in a garment may be forgotten and fall in the bathroom, which would disgrace them.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא means garment and hand together
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא corrects the reading. רבי עקיבא means he holds the תפילין in his hand, wrapped in his garment.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: He holds them in his garment and in his hand, and goes in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by changing the wording. The hand holds them securely, and the garment covers them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Gripping them in his hand solves the worry about falling. Covering them with the garment adds respect, so they are not exposed in the bathroom. In this reading, רבי עקיבא adds to בית הלל's view rather than rejecting it.
steps.whatToRemember: The final picture: according to רבי עקיבא, one enters holding the תפילין in his hand, covered by his garment.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
He holds them in his garment and in his hand, and enters.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 23 by rereading רבי עקיבא's words.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי עקיבא allows simply tucking the תפילין into one's clothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: He means holding them in the hand, covered by the garment, so they will not fall and are not exposed.

steps.title: Place them in holes by the bathroom, not by the public street
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says to place the תפילין in holes next to the בית הכסא, not in holes facing the רשות הרבים, because passersby may take them and he will come under suspicion.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he places them in the holes next to the bathroom. He should not place them in the holes next to the public domain, because passersby might take them and he will come to be suspected.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues and tells us where a person should leave his תפילין when he goes into the בית הכסא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two possible spots are compared: holes by the בית הכסא and holes facing the street. The street spot is ruled out because of a new worry, חשד (suspicion). If strangers take the תפילין, people may suspect the owner of something improper.

keyTerms.meaning: Holes or niches in the wall

phrases.english: And he places them in the holes next to the bathroom,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא יַנִּיחֵם בַּחוֹרִין הַסְּמוּכִים לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים,
phrases.english: but he should not place them in the holes next to the public domain,
lest passersby take them,
phrases.notes: The danger is that strangers will walk off with them.

phrases.english: and he will come to be suspected.
phrases.notes: The next step's story shows what this suspicion could look like.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא after the method of holding the תפילין was clarified, now addressing where to leave them.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Put the תפילין in holes by the בית הכסא, not in holes facing the street, because of theft and suspicion.

steps.title: The tragic story of the student and the stolen תפילין
steps.stepSummary: A student left his תפילין in a hole facing the street. A זונה took them and falsely claimed in the בית המדרש that he gave them to her as payment. Out of shame, the student threw himself from a roof and died.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a story about a student who put his תפילין in holes next to the public street. A prostitute came and took them. She came to the בית המדרש and said, 'Look what so-and-so gave me as my payment!' When that student heard this, he went up to the roof, fell, and died.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא tells a real story that shows the danger it just warned about, the חשד from leaving תפילין by the street.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story turns the abstract worry of 'suspicion' into something concrete and terrible. The stolen תפילין became false 'evidence' of a sin. The shame was so great that the student took his own life, and this explains why the Sages took the risk so seriously.

keyTerms.meaning: An incident or story brought to teach a law

phrases.english: And there was an incident with one student

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהִנִּיחַ תְּפִילָּיו בַּחוֹרִין הַסְּמוּכִים לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים,
phrases.english: who placed his tefillin in the holes next to the public domain,
and a certain prostitute came and took them,
and she came to the study hall and said:

phrases.aramaic: רְאוּ מַה נָּתַן לִי פְּלוֹנִי בִּשְׂכָרִי!
phrases.english: See what so-and-so gave me as my payment!
phrases.notes: A false claim. The תפילין look like proof that he paid her.

phrases.english: When that student heard this,
he went up to the top of the roof, fell, and died.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the חשד warned about in step 25 with a real event.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Leaving תפילין by the public street once led to a false accusation and a tragic death.

steps.title: The enactment to hold the תפילין when entering
steps.stepSummary: Because of that story, the Sages enacted that a person holds his תפילין in his garment and in his hand as he enters.
steps.simpleTranslation: At that time they made an enactment that a person should hold them in his garment and in his hand, and then go in.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא concludes the story with the new rule it caused: stop leaving the תפילין outside and keep them with you.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This enactment removes the problem completely. If he never leaves the תפילין behind, nobody can take them. Note that the method, 'in his garment and in his hand', matches the corrected reading of רבי עקיבא in step 24.
steps.whatToRemember: Leaving תפילין outside led to tragedy, so the Sages ruled that a person keeps them with him, held in his hand and wrapped in his garment.

phrases.english: At that time they enacted
that he should hold them in his garment and in his hand, and enter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: States the practical result of the story in step 26.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: One holds the תפילין in his hand, wrapped in his garment, and enters with them.

steps.title: A second ברייתא: how the practice changed in stages
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא gives the history. At first, people put the תפילין in holes near the בית הכסא, but mice took them. Then they put them in windows facing the public, but passersby took them. Finally, the Sages enacted holding them in the hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: At first they used to put תפילין in holes next to the bathroom, and mice would come and take them. So they enacted that they put them in windows next to the public street, and passersby would come and take them. So they enacted that a person holds them in his hand and goes in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא that tells, step by step, how the practice changed over time until it reached the final rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each spot had its own problem. Near the בית הכסא there were mice, and by the street there were thieves. This explains why both 'leave them outside' options from the earlier opinions were dropped. The only safe answer left was to hold them.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the order. Holes by the בית הכסא came FIRST, and the mice problem caused the move to the street windows. In step 25 the street was rejected because of suspicion. Both spots failed, which is why the final rule is to hold them.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
At first they used to place tefillin
in the holes next to the bathroom,
and mice would come and take them.
They enacted that they should place them
in the windows next to the public domain;
and passersby would come and take them.
They enacted that he should hold them in his hand and enter.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: בָּרִאשׁוֹנָה הָיוּ מַנִּיחִין תְּפִילִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel ברייתא that explains through history why the final practice is to hold the תפילין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After both resting spots failed, the final enactment is to hold the תפילין in the hand when entering.

steps.title: How exactly to hold them: rolled up, in the right hand, by the heart
steps.stepSummary: רבי מיאשא, son of רבי יהושע בן לוי, gives the הלכה: roll the תפילין up like a scroll and hold them in the right hand opposite the heart.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מיאשא, son of רבי יהושע בן לוי, said: The הלכה is that he rolls them up like a scroll and holds them in his right hand, opposite his heart.
steps.whatsHappening: Now that we know he holds the תפילין, an אמורא tells us the proper way to hold them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds practical detail to 'hold them in his hand'. Rolling the straps around them like a scroll keeps them neat and compact. Holding them in the right hand by the heart treats them with respect.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא, son of רבי יהושע בן לוי

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי מְיָאשָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Meyasha, son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, said:
The halacha is: he rolls them up like a scroll,
phrases.notes: The straps are wound around the boxes.

phrases.english: and holds them in his right hand, opposite his heart.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי מְיָאשָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי: הֲלָכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the practical method for the enactment of holding the תפילין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Roll the תפילין like a scroll and hold them in the right hand opposite the heart.

steps.title: The strap must not hang down a handbreadth
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן (quoted by רב יוסף בר מניומי) adds a condition: no strap may hang out a טפח below the hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף בר מניומי said in the name of רב נחמן: This is only provided that a strap does not stick out a טפח from under his hand.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן adds a final condition to how the תפילין are held.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holding them correctly is not enough if a long piece of strap dangles down. A strap hanging a טפח or more is not properly controlled, and it could drag or touch something unclean. So the whole set must be held tightly together.
steps.whatToRemember: Final practice: roll the תפילין like a scroll, hold them in the right hand by the heart, wrapped in the garment, and make sure no strap hangs out a טפח below the hand.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן:
phrases.english: Rav Yosef bar Manyumi said that Rav Nachman said:
Provided that a strap does not
stick out from under his hand a handbreadth.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: וּבִלְבַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a limiting condition to רבי מיאשא's method.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The תפילין must be held fully in hand, with no strap hanging out a טפח.

steps.title: What changes when there is no time left to wear them
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא limits the earlier instruction to hold the תפילין: it applies when there is still time to put them on that day. Otherwise, the person puts them in a pouch a טפח in size.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יעקב בר אחא said in the name of רבי זירא: The earlier instruction applies only when there is time left in the day to put the תפילין on. If there is not, he makes a pouch a טפח in size for them and puts them there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא qualifies the rule about holding the תפילין. It gives a different way to keep them when the day is almost over.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If there is time to wear the תפילין again, he keeps them ready in his hand. If there is no time left, he places them in a pouch instead; this statement specifies that the pouch is a טפח.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב בַּר אַחָא אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Ya’akov bar Aḥa said in the name of Rabbi Zeira:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁיֵּשׁ שְׁהוּת בְּיוֹם לְלׇבְשָׁן,
phrases.english: They taught this only when there is time in the day to put them on,
but if there is no time in the day to put them on—

phrases.aramaic: עוֹשֶׂה לָהֶן כְּמִין כִּיס טֶפַח, וּמַנִּיחָן.
phrases.english: he makes a pouch a handbreadth in size for them and puts them in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁיֵּשׁ שְׁהוּת בְּיוֹם לְלׇבְשָׁן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a time-of-day limit to the earlier instruction to hold the תפילין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When there is no time left that day to put on the תפילין, place them in a pouch a טפח in size rather than holding them as previously described.

steps.title: Holding them by day and using a pouch at night
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן states the day-and-night distinction directly: hold the rolled תפילין opposite the heart by day, and put them in a pouch a טפח in size at night.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: By day, roll the תפילין like a scroll and hold them in the hand opposite the heart. At night, make a pouch a טפח in size for them and put them in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second statement that spells out what to do by day and what to do at night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The daytime instruction matches the earlier way of holding the תפילין. The nighttime instruction uses a pouch instead.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Ḥana said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan:
By day, he rolls them up like a scroll
and holds them in his hand opposite his heart,

phrases.aramaic: וּבַלַּיְלָה עוֹשֶׂה לָהֶן כְּמִין כִּיס טֶפַח,
phrases.english: and at night he makes a pouch a handbreadth in size for them,
and puts them in it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: States the day-and-night distinction explicitly after the previous step's distinction based on time remaining.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: By day, hold the rolled תפילין opposite the heart; at night, put them in a pouch a טפח in size.

steps.title: When the pouch must be a handbreadth
steps.stepSummary: אביי limits the טפח requirement to the regular container for the תפילין. A container not normally used for them may be smaller.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: The size requirement was taught only for a container that is their regular container. For a container that is not their regular container, even less than a טפח is enough.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now narrows the pouch-size rule. אביי distinguishes between the regular container for the תפילין and a different container.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous statements required a pouch a טפח in size. אביי says that size applies to the usual container, but not to one that is not usually used for these תפילין.

keyTerms.meaning: in a container that is their regular container
in a container that is not their regular container

phrases.english: Abaye said: They taught this only
for a container that is their regular container,
but for a container that is not their regular container,
even less than a handbreadth is enough.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בִּכְלִי שֶׁהוּא כִּלְיָין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the pouch-size requirement stated in the two previous steps.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The טפח requirement applies to the תפילין’s regular container; a different container can be smaller.

steps.title: A small vessel shows that size is not always decisive
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא, or according to another attribution רב אשי, supports the distinction by pointing to small vessels that protect their contents in a tent containing a corpse.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא—and some say רב אשי—said: Consider this: small vessels protect their contents even in a tent containing a corpse.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for אביי’s distinction. It points to another case where a small container still provides protection.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The example shows why a container need not always be a טפח to provide separation. It supports allowing a smaller container here; it does not say that every container has the same rules.

keyTerms.meaning: consider this; an introduction to supporting evidence

steps.whatToRemember: The final distinction is about which container is used: the regular container needs a טפח, while a different container can be smaller.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר מָר זוּטְרָא, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Mar Zutra said, and some say Rav Ashi:
Consider this: small vessels
protect their contents in a tent containing a corpse.

steps.triggerLanguage: תֵּדַע שֶׁהֲרֵי פַּכִּין קְטַנִּים מַצִּילִין בְּאֹהֶל הַמֵּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies supporting evidence for אביי’s allowance of a container smaller than a טפח.
steps.raayaObject: A small container can sometimes provide protection despite being smaller than a טפח.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The rule that small vessels protect their contents in an אֹהֶל הַמֵּת.

steps.title: He handed over one item but kept the תפילין
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה reports that רבי יוחנן handed his students a book of אגדה before entering the בית הכסא, but did not hand them his תפילין.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said: When we walked behind רבי יוחנן, if he wanted to enter the bathroom while holding a book of אגדה, he would give it to us. If he was holding תפילין, he would not give them to us.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports what רבי יוחנן did in two similar situations. This contrast sets up his explanation in the next line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The setting is the same: רבי יוחנן is about to enter the בית הכסא. What changes is the item in his hand, and his response changes with it.

keyTerms.meaning: he would give it to us

phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Hana said:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֲוָה אָזְלִינַן בָּתְרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן,
phrases.english: When we would walk behind Rabbi Yohanan,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֲוָה בָּעֵי לְמֵיעַל לְבֵית הַכִּסֵּא
phrases.english: when he wanted to enter the bathroom
if he was holding a book of aggadic teachings—
he would give it to us,
but if he was holding phylacteries—
he would not give them to us,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the discussion of how to protect תפילין, the גמרא turns to an observed practice involving רבי יוחנן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The report records רבי יוחנן’s different treatment of a book of אגדה and תפילין; it has not yet completed his reason.

steps.title: His reason begins with permission from the חכמים
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן begins explaining his treatment of the תפילין by pointing to permission granted by חכמים, but the sentence stops before saying what follows from that permission.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Since the חכמים permitted them—
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins רבי יוחנן’s explanation for not handing over the תפילין. The explanation is unfinished on this amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words introduce a reason based on permission from חכמים. They do not yet state the full reason or its conclusion, so this line should not be read as a complete ruling.

phrases.english: He said: Since the sages permitted them—
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This begins to explain the difference in רבי יוחנן’s behavior reported in step 35.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יוחנן invokes permission from חכמים, but this passage does not finish his statement.
